routes.description: Establish sufficient warrant for Christianity by defending appropriate historical and relational modes of inquiry, the credibility of the Gospel portrayal of Jesus, the resurrection inference, and Christianity's account of moral meaning and human value.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative case gives adequate reason to trust the central Christian claims, especially Jesus's identity and resurrection, while showing that documentary, scientific, moral, and rival-religion objections do not defeat that warrant.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defended evidence for Jesus and the resurrection, together with Christianity's explanatory claims, to sufficient warrant for Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Justify using historical, documentary, and relational reasoning without treating scientific repeatability as the sole avenue to truth.
Establish that the Gospel sources preserve a sufficiently coherent and historically credible portrayal of Jesus.
Show that the reported death, empty tomb, appearances, and witness transformation are better explained by resurrection than by relevant alternatives.
Explain objective morality, human value, suffering, and human wrongdoing within a coherent Christian account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify criteria intended to distinguish Christian claims from incompatible religious claims rather than validating them symmetrically.
Distinguish Christianity's normative commitments from disputed interpretations, divine accommodation, and human misuse of scripture.

routes.description: Show that Christianity has not met its burden because its verification methods do not reliably distinguish truth from fiction or rival religions, its sources do not establish their supernatural claims, and its accounts of morality and human value face viable secular alternatives and textual objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proffered methods and evidence remain insufficient to establish the Gospel and resurrection claims, especially when tested against ordinary evidential standards, alternative explanations, internal disputes, and the distinction between transmission and truth.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved evidential and explanatory deficits to withholding affirmation that Christianity is true or sufficiently warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require truth-testing criteria that discriminate Christianity from incompatible religions, fiction, and unsupported supernatural explanations.
Separate textual preservation, consistency, and accurate background details from evidence that the Gospel claims correspond to reality.
Show that resurrection testimony and proposed historical facts do not justify a supernatural bodily-resurrection inference.
Test claims about divine moral grounding and equal human value against secular accounts and morally difficult biblical provisions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that identifying defects in an affirmative method does not require supplying a method that verifies supernatural claims.
Apply empirical scrutiny to asserted physical events even when those events are presented through historical or religious narratives.

sections.title: Truth-Testing Methods and Evidential Burdens
sections.rationale: This issue governs what would count as sufficient warrant, whether Christianity can be distinguished from rival claims, and whether criticism of an offered method incurs a separate positive burden.

sections.title: Gospel Preservation, Coherence, and Historical Reliability
sections.rationale: The Gospel documents are the principal route to claims about Jesus, so the distinction between textual transmission, literary and archaeological indicators, narrative coherence, and factual truth is central.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: The resurrection is presented as Christianity's decisive truth condition, making the death, burial, empty tomb, appearances, witnesses, narrative disagreements, and natural or supernatural explanations the largest issue.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Human Value, and Meaning
sections.rationale: The motion expressly concerns moral meaning and human value, requiring comparison of the proposed divine grounding with secular sources of meaning and moral regard.

sections.title: Scriptural Morality, Creation, Evil, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Claims about creation, gender, slavery, suffering, interpretation, accommodation, and free will test whether Christianity's texts and moral framework remain coherent with its account of divine goodness.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Human beings possess value because they are created in God's image, loved by God, and offered eternal life through Christ.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains part of Cliffe's uninterrupted opening statement and is framed through his own expressly Christian explanation of human worth.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies Christianity's proposed explanation of human value and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a material explanatory contribution, though the supporting bridge is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The value claim and its Christian grounds are recoverable, with the metaphysical status of the explanation left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The passage confidently presents divine creation and love as the explanation without defending those factual premises here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the stated Christian premises hold, the value conclusion follows intelligibly, but the grounding relation is only asserted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage provides theological assertions rather than independent support for creation, divine love, or eternal life.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral-account bridge by offering a Christian ground for equal human worth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its own positive account and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grounds human value in creation in God's image, divine love, purpose, and offered eternal life.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Objective good and evil require a mind prior to human minds that creates and defines moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement and Cliffe's repeated first-person framing clearly attribute this moral argument to him.

response.rationale: This is a constructive moral-grounding argument and does not purport to answer any earlier locked opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a direct central thesis but compresses the decisive necessity inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but objective, real, creates, and defines are not sufficiently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim exceeds the support supplied because competing non-theistic accounts of moral objectivity are not addressed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion depends on an unsupported conditional that objective values can exist only if created by a prior mind.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Appeals to conscience support moral experience but do not establish the exclusive metaphysical explanation asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The claim directly supports the indispensable Christian moral-grounding step in the pro route.

representationalCharity.rationale: No opposing moral theory is described sufficiently for a meaningful source-supported charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites the speakers' consciences and infers that real good and evil require a value-defining prior mind.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: The resurrection claim should be evaluated through historical and relational evidence, together with logic and reason, rather than through scientific evidence alone.
moves.attributionBasis: Cliffe presents this sustained evidential argument during his uninterrupted opening, with no speaker ambiguity in the delivered rows.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the pro side's proposed evidential framework and has no earlier opposing move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly identifies several permissible modes of inquiry and their intended domains.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological proposition is clear, though the standards governing relational evidence remain implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The plural-method point is well motivated, but the passage does not show that each form reliably supports resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples coherently show that scientific testing is not the sole rational mode of inquiry, with one implicit applicability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The love analogy supports evidential pluralism but does not verify the reliability of historical or relational resurrection evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central methodological bridge by rejecting scientific repeatability as the exclusive truth standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move contrasts evidential domains without developing a sufficiently specific opposing position for testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes scientific, historical, relational, philosophical, logical, and reason-based forms of evidence.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A method cannot establish Christianity as true if its consistent application equally verifies mutually incompatible religions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Matt the floor for his opening, and this methodological argument proceeds continuously in Matt's first-person presentation.

components.text: Whether the proposed non-scientific methods can reliably establish Christianity rather than incompatible claims.

response.rationale: The reply identifies non-discrimination as the defect in the proposed methodology and states that symmetric verification of incompatible religions prevents it from establishing Christianity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive methodological inference is expressly challenged and its truth-testing consequence is clearly stated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional criticism is clear, stable, and expressly limited to methods that verify incompatible claims equally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a conditional demand for discrimination, the asserted force matches the logical incompatibility identified.

charity.alternative: Different kinds of evidence may legitimately apply to historical and relational questions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those kinds still need criteria that distinguish Christianity from mutually incompatible religious conclusions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If one method equally warrants incompatible conclusions, it cannot by itself establish one of them as true.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological critique is strongly warranted, though the excerpt does not document particular rival applications in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central con-method requirement for a discriminating truth test.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accepts evidential pluralism in principle while accurately retaining the decisive discrimination requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts a shared correspondence conception of truth and asks how Christian claims can actually be verified.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Without empirical support for the claimed physical event, a resurrection cannot responsibly be affirmed, and ignorance of a natural explanation does not demonstrate a supernatural one.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt develops this extended epistemic argument without interruption during his opening statement, making the speaker attribution unambiguous.

components.text: Whether historical and relational evidence can responsibly warrant affirmation of a physical resurrection.
Whether lack of a known natural explanation supplies positive support for a supernatural explanation.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the applicability of plural evidence to a physical resurrection and directly rejects an inference from unexplained events to supernatural causation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both decisive epistemic components, but the empirical-only formulation does not fully engage historical inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-versus-supernatural inference is clear, but the required scope of empirical support is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately frames the conclusion as withholding affirmation and acknowledges limits in known explanations.

charity.alternative: Historical testimony can sometimes justify belief in physical events without repeatable laboratory evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Extraordinary supernatural causation still requires support beyond ignorance of an available natural explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rejection of an argument from ignorance is coherent, though empirical support is not the only possible historical warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic principle is well defended conceptually, but no detailed comparison with the actual resurrection reports is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con-resurrection bridge against a supernatural bodily-resurrection inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the possibility of reports while fairly insisting that explanatory ignorance is insufficient.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes reports of unexplained experiences from demonstrations that a supernatural cause is most plausible.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Jesus's reported death, known burial, postmortem appearances, transformed witnesses, and later conversions constitute a cumulative historical case for his resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle begins by expressly identifying the evidence for the resurrection and then gives a continuous catalogue of supporting claims.

components.text: What positive historical support, beyond explanatory ignorance, warrants a resurrection inference.
Whether the proposed evidence distinguishes the Christian resurrection claim from unsupported religious claims.

response.rationale: The catalogue supplies purported positive facts responsive to the evidential deficit, but it does not answer the discrimination demand or compare serious natural alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive evidential component is contacted, while the alternative-comparison and discrimination components remain unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is recoverable, but the reported status and independence of each item remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The catalogue is presented as powerful resurrection evidence without adequate source defense or rival comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The facts could cumulatively support resurrection, but the bridge from reports and transformations to supernatural causation is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claims depend heavily on Gospel reports and asserted witness transformations without defending independence, verification, or alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable pro resurrection bridge through an enumerated historical case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily presents a positive catalogue and does not substantially characterize a specific opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage cites reported death, burial, an identifiable tomb, appearances, transformed witnesses, and later conversions.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even nearly perfect reconstruction and preservation of an original Gospel text would not establish that the claims written in that text correspond to reality.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly discusses the absence of originals, comparison among surviving copies, reconstruction uncertainty, and the separate question of truth.

components.text: Whether accurately preserved reports establish that the reported resurrection-related facts correspond to reality.

response.rationale: The reply contacts a documentary warrant underlying the cumulative case by separating reconstruction of what was written from truth of what was reported.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It decisively contacts the preservation-to-truth bridge but does not assess every historical item in the cumulative case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between textual reconstruction and correspondence truth is explicitly and stably formulated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion accurately states that preservation alone cannot demonstrate the original claims' truth.

charity.alternative: Excellent manuscript preservation can establish with confidence what an original source said.
charity.decisiveQualification: Knowing what a source said does not by itself establish that its assertions correspond to reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between accurate transmission and factual truth is explicit, valid, and unaffected by granting near-perfect reconstruction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual point needs little empirical support, though the manuscript uncertainty is only briefly described.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central con-documents distinction between preservation and correspondence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the strongest preservation premise and isolates the exact remaining evidential qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grants near-identity with an original text and denies that this demonstrates the original claims.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Literary form, manuscript preservation, archaeological corroboration, and internal consistency jointly support treating the Gospels as historically reliable.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle explicitly enumerates four tests he applies to historical books and then applies each test to the New Testament Gospels.

components.text: What considerations beyond manuscript preservation support correspondence or historical reliability.
Whether the proposed tests discriminate truthful history from incompatible or fictional narratives.

response.rationale: Literary form, archaeology, and internal consistency add considerations beyond preservation, but the move does not establish that these tests discriminate truth from convincing fiction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the primary preservation-versus-truth demand but leaves the decisive discrimination challenge unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The four tests are clear, but historically reliable shifts between background accuracy, consistency, and broader factual truth.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The tests support some reliability indicators but do not warrant the broad historical conclusion as confidently asserted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference conflates useful reliability indicators with sufficient grounds for broad historical truth and denies contradictions categorically.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage names manuscript, archaeological, literary, and consistency considerations but provides limited representative verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro-Gospels bridge with an expressly cumulative reliability case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move enumerates positive tests without presenting a developed opposing interpretation for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: Knechtle enumerates literary genre, manuscript preservation, archaeology, and internal harmony as four historical tests.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Literary style, manuscript preservation, accurate place-names, and internal consistency cannot establish Gospel truth because fictional narratives can satisfy all four criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty systematically follows Knechtle's four stated criteria, tests each criterion, and concludes that the methodology is incapable of establishing truth.

components.text: Whether the four reliability tests establish that Gospel claims correspond to reality.
Whether accurate settings, preserved wording, suitable style, and consistency discriminate history from fiction.

response.rationale: The reply tests each proposed criterion, identifies its compatibility with fiction as the defect, and concludes that the method cannot establish the narrative's truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central inference and all four supporting criteria, then states the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compatibility claim is precisely conditional and does not deny that the tests can support narrower conclusions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is properly limited to insufficiency: fiction compatibility prevents the four tests alone from establishing truth.

charity.alternative: The four indicators can cumulatively increase confidence that a document is historically serious and informed.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even cumulatively, those indicators do not entail that extraordinary narrative claims correspond to reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Demonstrating that all four criteria are compatible with fiction directly defeats their sufficiency as a truth test.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general counterexamples are representative and apt, with only limited detailed application to particular Gospel passages.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con-documents bridge by separating reliability indicators from factual truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply allows the criteria's narrower evidential value while correctly preserving the decisive insufficiency qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains that accurate places, faithful manuscripts, suitable style, and consistency can all occur in false stories.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Once an offered truth-testing method is shown defective, the critic need not supply a replacement or a method that confirms supernatural claims.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty resumes after the moderator's intervention and directly explains why rebutting Knechtle's method creates no obligation to replace it.

components.text: Whether exposing defects in the offered reliability method obliges the critic to provide a better method.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the burden-shifting inference as invalid and states that a critic may reject a flawed method without repairing the advocate's foundation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The burden demand is expressly identified, rejected on principle, and linked to the consequence for the offered method.

precisionFindings.rationale: The procedural claim is clear and limited to criticism of an advocate's offered truth-testing method.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The allocation of burden is stated categorically but appropriately for the limited task of exposing insufficiency.

charity.alternative: A critic's alternative method could help show that the dispute is constructive rather than merely skeptical.
charity.decisiveQualification: Usefulness of an alternative does not make supplying one necessary to demonstrate a defect in the offered method.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows from the distinction between defeating an offered method and assuming responsibility for replacing it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden principle is directly supported by the described dialectical situation and requires little additional factual evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary con burden bridge and sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes the possible value of replacement from an alleged obligation to provide it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says exposing the offered methodology's problem does not create a duty to fix or replace the advocate's foundation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: An empty tomb and reported appearances would not alone justify resurrection because late transmitted accounts can acquire embellished details without any conspiracy.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Matt, and the uninterrupted first-person answer continues until the next audience question begins.

components.text: Whether an empty tomb and reported postmortem appearances sufficiently justify bodily resurrection.
Whether late transmission and embellishment can explain narrative detail without a deliberate conspiracy.

response.rationale: The reply grants the relevant facts conditionally, requests specific accounts, and supplies late embellishment as an alternative to resurrection without alleging conspiracy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive inference and offers a relevant alternative, though the alternative is not developed in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully conditional on an empty tomb and appearances and limited to their insufficiency.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses appropriately cautious language and identifies what additional account-specific evidence would be needed.

charity.alternative: A known empty tomb plus sincere postmortem appearances could form a serious cumulative historical case.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those facts still underdetermine bodily resurrection when late transmission and embellishment remain live possibilities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination argument is coherent, though mere possibility of embellishment does not establish its comparative probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Late embellishment is a plausible rival but is asserted without detailed dating, transmission, or comparative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con-resurrection bridge by challenging the bodily-resurrection inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply conditionally grants the strongest stated facts and identifies the precise remaining inferential gap.

moves.evidenceBasis: The answer conditionally grants an empty tomb and appearances but asks for account details and raises later embellishment.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Christian faith calls for evidence-seeking skepticism rather than blind credulity, while inquiry should examine competing accounts of meaning, ethics, and value.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator expressly gives Cliffe the response, after which a continuous answer defines cynicism and skepticism until Matt begins his rebuttal.

components.text: Whether a critic must supply a replacement method or positive worldview after exposing an offered method's defects.
Whether Christian inquiry should examine evidence rather than rely on blind faith.

response.rationale: The move advocates evidence-seeking skepticism but does not answer the burden-allocation argument; its demand that the critic offer an account restates the disputed burden.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contains relevant contrary material but leaves the primary burden objection uncontacted and answers only an adjacent evidential concern.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between skepticism and cynicism is recoverable, but hyperskepticism lacks an operational threshold.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The general call to examine evidence is fitting, while the implied obligation to supply alternatives is insufficiently warranted.

charity.alternative: A critic may reasonably withhold belief after identifying defects without offering a complete rival worldview.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refusing a positive replacement is not by itself cynical or evidence-resistant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Evidence-seeking skepticism is coherent, but the move equivocates between constructive inquiry and a duty to replace defeated claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The normative appeal to study evidence is reasonable, but no support is supplied for labeling nonreplacement hyperskeptical.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly attacks the subsidiary con burden bridge, though it does not successfully engage its inferential basis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The cynicism framing materially weakens the critic's burden position by omitting its decisive procedural qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects blind faith, endorses hard questions and evidence, and criticizes skeptics who offer no alternative account.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Human beings can have reasons to regard people as meaningful and valuable without belief in God, while textual fidelity does not establish Christianity's truth.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience prompt names Matt, and the ensuing extended answer explicitly discusses Cliffe's four points before ending at the moderator's transition.

components.text: Whether belief in creation in God's image is necessary for reasons to value human beings.
Whether textual fidelity or authorial intent establishes Christianity's truth.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies that divine-image belief is required for human meaning and separately reiterates that textual accuracy does not establish Christianity's truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both relevant components, though the positive secular grounding of value remains only briefly stated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to having reasons for value without God rather than establishing a universal secular foundation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest existential claim that nonbelievers can possess reasons for human value fits the support offered.

charity.alternative: The divine-image account proposes an objective metaphysical ground rather than merely a person's reasons for valuing others.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing secular reasons exist does not by itself answer whether either account supplies objective value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The existence of secular reasons coherently defeats a necessity claim, while not resolving the deeper ontological comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal possession of reasons is directly supported, but their content and adequacy are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con moral-adequacy bridge by presenting a viable secular source of human regard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly denies necessity but leaves the strongest objective-grounding distinction somewhat compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that both speakers have reasons for human meaning and value and denies that textual intent decides truth.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Differing Gospel reports are not contradictory when they offer compatible but incomplete perspectives rather than mutually exclusive assertions.
moves.attributionBasis: After the alleged infancy contradiction is presented, Cliffe answers continuously with a two-witness collision analogy before Matt adds agreement.

components.text: Whether apparent Gospel differences are genuine contradictions or compatible incomplete reports.
Whether compatibility among accounts establishes that their reported events correspond to reality.

response.rationale: The analogy contacts the contradiction component by showing how differing details may coexist, but it does not answer fiction compatibility or establish factual truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers a secondary consistency component while leaving the decisive truth-discrimination component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The logical possibility is clear, but the move does not specify which Gospel reports satisfy compatibility constraints.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The collision analogy adequately establishes possibility of compatible perspectives, not their actual compatibility in every case.

charity.alternative: Some differing reports may make mutually exclusive assertions rather than merely omit different details.
charity.decisiveQualification: A generic analogy cannot settle compatibility without applying it to the exact disputed propositions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Different nonexclusive details can plainly be compatible, with the application to actual Gospel propositions left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy demonstrates a logical possibility but supplies no detailed textual comparison establishing actual compatibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con-documents challenge concerning inconsistency, but only on one component.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly illustrates its interpretation but leaves the strongest case-specific qualification unstated.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses two collision witnesses reporting different nonexclusive details to illustrate compatible perspectives.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Appeals to creation or divorce do not resolve biblical rules that treat men and women unequally in marriage, remarriage, inheritance, and valuation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly turns back to Knechtle's Matthew 19 answer and advances Dillahunty's previously stated critique of biblical inequality.

components.text: Whether Christianity's equal-value claim is coherent with unequal biblical treatment of men and women.
Whether differing textual rules can be treated as merely compatible perspectives rather than substantive inequality.

response.rationale: The reply tests the abstract equal-value claim against concrete differences in divorce, remarriage, inheritance, and valuation rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive moral-consistency demand with several examples, though the excerpt does not document each rule fully.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection identifies specific domains of unequal treatment and does not claim that every biblical statement is unequal.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited rule differences support the critique, but absolute claims about valuation require fuller textual demonstration.

charity.alternative: Equal intrinsic value can coexist with differentiated social roles or legal rules.
charity.decisiveQualification: That distinction requires justification where the rules impose asymmetric rights, release, remarriage, or valuation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Using asymmetric rules to challenge an unqualified equality account is coherent, though inequality of treatment need not entail unequal intrinsic value.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete textual domains are identified, but quotations and contextual defenses are not supplied in this excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con moral-adequacy bridge by testing equal-value claims against scripture.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the conceptual distinction while pressing the specific inequalities that still require explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage cites different rules for divorce, remarriage, inheritance, and valuation as evidence of gender inequality.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: Divorce, slavery, polygamy, and sexism reflect accommodation to human hardness rather than God's ideal of equal human value presented before the fall.
moves.attributionBasis: Knechtle explicitly corrects the characterization of his prior argument and then restates his Genesis-and-fall distinction in a continuous turn.

components.text: How unequal biblical practices can coexist with a Christian ideal of equal human value.
Whether the specific asymmetric rules are morally justified or merely accommodated.

response.rationale: The creation-versus-accommodation distinction answers the general compatibility challenge but does not explain or justify the specific unequal provisions identified.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive interpretive premise while leaving the concrete rule-level moral demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between divine ideal and permitted accommodation is expressly stated and consistently applied.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted status of every listed practice as mere accommodation is not established by the cited divorce phrase alone.

charity.alternative: Biblical regulation of unequal practices may implicate divine moral approval rather than mere human misuse.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling a practice nonideal must still explain why the text authorizes or regulates its harmful forms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Accommodation can reconcile permission with a contrary ideal, but the extension from divorce to all listed practices is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Matthew 19 supports an accommodation reading of divorce but does not by itself establish the same reading for slavery or sexism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro interpretation bridge and occupies the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the moral objection but omits its decisive challenge concerning divine authorization and regulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes hardness of heart and pre-fall equality to distinguish permitted practices from God's ideal.

moves.speaker: Cliffe Knechtle
moves.proposition: God's creation of meaningful human freedom permits people to corrupt the good creation, so human atrocities are attributable to human misuse of freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator returns the audience's intervention question to Knechtle, who answers directly using his characteristic free-will defense.

components.text: Whether morally difficult biblical provisions are attributable to divine rules rather than merely human wrongdoing.
Whether human misuse of freedom can explain atrocities committed by human agents.

response.rationale: The free-will defense addresses human-caused evil generally but does not contact the locked objection concerning unequal rules within scripture.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies issue-bearing moral material while leaving the selected decisive scriptural component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The human-evil claim is clear, with the boundaries of meaningful freedom and divine prevention left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Free choice plausibly explains some human wrongdoing, but the passage presents it as broadly sufficient without addressing constraints.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Meaningful freedom coherently permits misuse, though the necessity and extent of permitted harm remain underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The defense supplies a familiar conceptual possibility but no evidence that all relevant atrocities require unrestricted prevention failures.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro moral-account bridge by attributing human atrocities to misuse of freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The short defense does not describe a sufficiently developed opposing account for meaningful charity testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that created free agents can pervert a good creation and attributes extensive corruption to humans.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Exodus prohibits kidnapping rather than slaveholding and, in the same chapter, regulates ownership, unequal release, and violent treatment of slaves.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn immediately answers Knechtle's citation of Exodus 21:16 and uses the detailed textual critique consistently advanced by Dillahunty earlier.

components.text: Whether Exodus's prohibition on man-stealing establishes opposition to slavery rather than only kidnapping.
Whether the surrounding chapter regulates ownership, unequal release, and violent treatment of slaves.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes kidnapping from slaveholding, identifies contrary regulations in the same chapter, and states why the cited prohibition does not establish opposition to slavery.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the cited premise, supplies contextual defeating material, and states the resulting failure of the inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between kidnapping and slaveholding is precise, and the claim is limited to the cited Exodus context.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that a kidnapping ban is not a slavery ban fits the textual distinction and surrounding regulations.

charity.alternative: A prohibition on kidnapping may constrain an important source of enslavement and express some protection for persons.
